content: Airway swelling and mucus plugging are the primary pathological features observed in infants suffering from acute viral bronchiolitis. Nebulised hypertonic saline solution, with a concentration of 3% or higher, has been proposed as a treatment to alleviate these pathological changes and reduce airway obstruction. This review, which was initially published in 2008 and subsequently updated in 2010, 2013, and 2017, evaluates the effects of nebulised hypertonic saline in infants with acute bronchiolitis. The review included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared nebulised hypertonic saline, either alone or combined with bronchodilators, to nebulised normal saline (0.9%) or standard treatment in children under 24 months of age with acute bronchiolitis. The primary outcome for hospitalised infants was the length of hospital stay, while for outpatients or emergency department (ED) patients, the primary outcome was the rate of hospitalisation. The updated review incorporated six new trials, bringing the total to 34 trials involving 5205 infants with acute bronchiolitis, of whom 2727 received hypertonic saline. Most trials used a 3% saline concentration, although six trials used concentrations ranging from 5% to 7%. The trials were conducted across various regions, including Asia, North America, South America, Europe, and the Mediterranean and Middle East. Funding sources were reported in only a subset of the trials, with some receiving government or academic funding, while others did not disclose funding information. The findings suggest that hospitalised infants treated with nebulised hypertonic saline may experience a slightly shorter average length of hospital stay compared to those treated with normal saline or standard care (mean difference: −0.40 days; 95% confidence interval: −0.69 to −0.11; low-certainty evidence). Additionally, infants receiving hypertonic saline may show lower clinical severity scores within the first three days of treatment compared to those receiving normal saline. On day 1, the mean difference in clinical scores was −0.64 (95% CI: −1.08 to −0.21); on day 2, it was −1.07 (95% CI: −1.60 to −0.53); and on day 3, it was −0.89 (95% CI: −1.44 to −0.34). These results are based on low-certainty evidence. For outpatients and ED patients, nebulised hypertonic saline may reduce the risk of hospitalisation by 13% compared to normal saline (risk ratio: 0.87; 95% CI: 0.78 to 0.97; low-certainty evidence). However, it does not appear to significantly reduce the risk of hospital readmission within 28 days after discharge (risk ratio: 0.83; 95% CI: 0.55 to 1.25; low-certainty evidence). The evidence regarding the time to resolution of symptoms such as wheezing, cough, and pulmonary moist crackles is uncertain. For wheezing, the mean difference was −1.16 days (95% CI: −1.43 to −0.89; very low-certainty evidence). For cough, the mean difference was −0.87 days (95% CI: −1.31 to −0.44; very low-certainty evidence). For pulmonary moist crackles, the mean difference was −1.30 days (95% CI: −2.28 to −0.32; very low-certainty evidence). Safety data were reported in 27 trials. Fourteen trials, involving 1624 infants (767 treated with hypertonic saline, 96% of whom also received bronchodilators), reported no adverse events. Thirteen trials, involving 2792 infants (1479 treated with hypertonic saline, 28% of whom received bronchodilators and 72% received hypertonic saline alone), reported at least one adverse event. These adverse events included worsening cough, agitation, bronchospasm, bradycardia, desaturation, vomiting, and diarrhea. Most adverse events were mild and resolved spontaneously (low-certainty evidence). In conclusion, nebulised hypertonic saline may modestly reduce the length of hospital stay in infants hospitalised with acute bronchiolitis and may slightly improve clinical severity scores. It may also reduce the risk of hospitalisation in outpatients and ED patients. The treatment appears to be safe, with only minor and self-limiting adverse events, particularly when administered alongside a bronchodilator. However, the certainty of the evidence for all outcomes is low to very low, primarily due to inconsistency and potential bias in the included studies.
